item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=onLuFYFwGok

值得閱讀的理由

  • 掌握從設計源頭化解居家危險的技巧，告別醜陋且難以清理的防撞貼條。
  • 了解兼顧安全監控與空氣品質的建材與格局規劃，大幅降低父母育兒焦慮。
  • 學習培養孩子自主收納的櫃體尺寸設計，以及隨年齡彈性調整的「輕裝修、重軟裝」概念。

摘要

從規劃根絕危險：邊角圓化與隱形防護

作者身為擁有三個孩子的空間設計師，指出許多新手父母常在孩子出生後才到處黏貼防撞膠條，未來拆除時極易毀損家具表面。作者建議在裝修規劃初期就將玄關、中島等動線上的尖銳邊角進行倒圓角設計，並全面採用無把手櫃體，避免幼童跌倒或奔跑時撞傷頭部與眼睛。此外，距地面30公分以下的插座應全面加裝安全蓋，以防幼童拿異物探索造成觸電危險。

地坪安全與隱形健康：防滑與低甲醛

五歲以下的孩童大部分時間都在地面活動，作者認為地面材質的安全與耐用至關重要。作者優先推薦具備高防滑與抗刮特性的超耐磨木地板，不僅能在孩子跌倒時提供緩衝，也能承受玩具車拖拉刮磨。除了看得見的建材，作者更提醒大眾注意看不見的甲醛危害，建議選用F1級低甲醛材料與無毒乳膠漆，守護呼吸道與免疫系統尚未發育完全的孩童健康。

開放式格局與塗鴉牆：緩解育兒焦慮與促進互動

父母在獨立廚房忙碌時，往往因看不見客廳的孩子而焦慮不安。作者提出採用開放式公領域設計（客廳、餐廳與廚房相連），並以中島作為輕隔間，讓家長在備餐料理時只要抬頭就能掌握孩子的動態。同時，作者建議在公領域留一面牆打造為黑板漆或白板塗鴉牆，給予孩子自由發揮的天地，使親子宅回歸自然互動的生活本質，而非冷冰冰的樣品屋。

分齡收納訓練：110公分的自主收拾黃金高度

面對玩具撒滿地的育兒日常，作者強調收納設計應以「訓練孩子自己收拾」為核心。作者將櫃體底層規劃為抽屜，並在110公分以下配置收納櫃或開放式層架搭配收納籃，讓孩子能輕鬆拿取與歸位。衣櫃部分，因應孩子身型抽高速度快，作者強烈建議捨棄固定式五金吊桿，改採活動式層板與可調式吊衣桿，以靈活調整空間，避免容量浪費。

彈性成長思維：輕裝修重軟裝的長遠規劃

許多家長常依當下喜好將兒童房打造成城堡或貼滿卡通壁紙，但幾年後孩子長大往往不再適用。作者建議兒童房應採取「輕裝修、重軟裝」的設計理念，硬裝維持簡約耐看，搭配可升降成長桌椅與基本款家具。將風格與配置的決定權留給未來長大的孩子，不仅能避免二次大裝修的困擾，更能打造出真正能陪伴孩子長大的理想住宅。

================================================

# 精彩預告

This is probably every parent's nightmare. You just finish tidying up their toys, and they go somewhere else and dump out another entire box. You’re cleaning up every day, and the more you clean, the worse your temper gets. My advice here is that because a child’s respiratory and immune systems are still developing, what you can’t see is actually more important than how good the materials look. The very last point, and one I think everyone easily overlooks, is reserving. space for their growth. Hi everyone, I’m Uncle. Let’s talk about family-friendly homes today. Many know I’m a designer, but they might not know I have three kids of my own; the youngest is three and the oldest is in fifth grade. So, I have quite a few insights on family-friendly homes to share with you all. Many homeowners I meet, when planning a home for their kids, immediately buy tons of anti-collision strips and corner protectors, and just start sticking them.

# Intro

everywhere. Then, when the kids grow up and you need to take them off, if you’re lucky, it’s just sticky residue. If you’re unlucky, you might rip off the paint or the finish of your furniture and cabinets. So, truly planning a family-friendly home isn’t about waiting until the kids are born to buy protectors; it’s about building safety, interaction, and future flexibility right into the design. Today, I’ve condensed my years of. renovation experience and living insights into five key points to share with you. There are. Parents know that when children first learn to walk, they are wobbly and off-balance. When they fall, the most dangerous thing in the home isn’t the floor, but the sharp corners—and not the kind of " corners" you eat. Okay? I mean the sharp edges. >> Those dumplings are delicious, though.

# 痛點 1：跌倒防護與尖角危機

Anyway, where do these sharp corners appear? Things like system cabinets, kitchen islands, entry corners, or high-traffic areas—anywhere you have these sharp edges, it’s easy to get hurt. My first suggestion is that during the planning phase, you should round off all corners in the entryway and on your kitchen island. Why do this rounding during the planning phase? If you decide early, it actually saves you a certain amount of money on labor later on. Sure, these rounded edges.

might cost a little bit more, but in terms of safety, I think the investment is absolutely worth it. Next is choosing handles for your cabinets. How should you choose them? Just go with handleless designs. Protruding handles can be dangerous when kids are crawling, standing, or running around; they might bump their heads or eyes, which can cause serious injuries. Another small detail is that when planning your outlets, I recommend installing safety covers on any outlet located lower than 30 centimeters from.

the floor. Because children sometimes try to play with those outlets using wires, their fingers, or even drool. Small. Children actually love playing on the floor. I should say that for kids under five, most of their time is spent playing on the floor, whether they're lying down, sitting, or standing—it’s all fun. >> Whenever things fall to the floor, they.

# 痛點 2：地面安全與看不見的隱形危機

almost always pick them up and put them right into their mouths. So, the material of the floor is very important . Besides being easy to clean, I personally prioritize high-slip-resistance wood flooring, like wear-resistant laminate. It provides a certain level of cushioning, so if a child falls, it won't hurt as much as hitting tiles. Also, since kids often drag toy cars around, durable and scratch-resistant wood makes maintenance much less of a hassle. Besides flooring materials,.

there's another thing people often overlook: formaldehyde. That’s why I recommend choosing F1-grade low-formaldehyde materials paired with non-toxic, eco-friendly latex paint. If you want even more peace of mind, you can have a professional formaldehyde removal service done for the whole house , since children's respiratory and immune systems are still developing. Things like air quality—these invisible factors—are actually more important than how nice your materials look.

Third. The third point is what I think can best reduce stress for parents. Anyone with kids knows that when it’s suddenly quiet, that’s when real trouble usually starts. For example, if you're cooking in a separate kitchen while the kids are playing in the living room, even if you’re in the kitchen, your mind will constantly be checking on them to see if they're safe. In reality, you can't even get your work done properly that way. I believe every parent has experienced this anxious feeling. My personal solution is to.

# 痛點 3：化解爸媽心理壓力！可穿透性公領域

incorporate more transparent or open designs into the space. For example, when designing homes for families, I often connect the living room, dining room, and kitchen, turning the latter into an open-concept space. If the area is large enough, I’ll even add a kitchen island as a divider. This way, whether you're cooking or prepping, you can just look up to see the kids playing without having to constantly peek around corners like before. Also, for the common area, I have a great design tip to boost interaction: I.

suggest picking a wall and turning it into a chalkboard or whiteboard, giving the kids a space where they’re allowed to doodle freely. I believe that this kind of genuine family interaction is the essence of family-friendly design, rather than creating something that just looks good but feels like a cold, impersonal model home. Simply put, I believe it’s in a child’s nature to be active. We shouldn't try to restrict them; instead, we should provide a safe space where they can fully express themselves .

This probably hits home as a nightmare for every parent. You finish tidying up their toys, and the next thing you know , they've dumped out another bin somewhere else. You end up cleaning all day, and the more you clean, the worse your temper gets. My suggestion here is meant to train children to clean up their own toys. The way I design the cabinetry is to make the bottom section a drawer, while the remaining space up to 110 centimeters becomes a storage cabinet or open shelving, where you can add storage bins later if you like.

# 痛點 4：終結收拾夢魘！自主收納櫃體規劃

Why set it at 110 centimeters? Because we’re talking about kids. If they still can't clean up after themselves by that height, it’s not a drawer issue, it’s an upbringing issue. But trust me, it’s not that simple, you just have to give them that kind of space. They won't get it right the first or second time, but they’ll eventually get used to it over time. Otherwise, you’ll be the one stuck cleaning up after them forever. This is truly a nightmare, I’m not lying. I have three kids, so I don't have that kind of time ; that’s why I have to train them from a. young age. Another thing is the closet. Kids 'clothing sizes change quickly, so never use fixed hardware rods. I highly recommend adjustable shelves or movable hanging rods, so you can easily adjust them as your child grows and their clothes get bigger, avoiding a lot of wasted, unusable space. Or The last point, which I think everyone.

# 痛點 5：被9成家長忽略的「成長預留空間」

easily overlooks, is leaving space for their future growth. Many people focus only on the present when planning a family home, usually just the next year or two, without realizing they might live there for 10, 15, or even 20 years , failing to account for future changes . Many new parents, full of love, turn their child’s room into a castle or use cartoon wallpaper; I’m not saying there's anything right or wrong with that. Because you are pouring your heart into it. But if we're being realistic, in five or.

ten years, they will inevitably look at that space and feel, "I’ve grown up now ." So, this is something you need to consider. If you plan to renovate the room again later on and just want to give them what they love at this stage, I think that’s fine. After all, if they are only two or three years old, setting it up like a serious college student's room would be quite strange. Therefore, I suggest adopting a "light.

renovation, heavy decor" design concept for children's rooms, such as height-adjustable desks and chairs, or simple, versatile bed frames and storage cabinets. When your child reaches middle school, high school, or college, you can let them choose the style they prefer. By leaving the decision-making to their future selves, you also avoid the trouble of having to undergo major renovations. The real point of a family home is to create a space that can grow with your.

# Ending

children without sacrificing your quality of life or aesthetic appeal. If you are also preparing to renovate your family home, feel free to tell me in the comments which of these points resonated with you the most, or which one gives you the most trouble? I’m J-Ju, see you next time, bye.
